questions.stem: Inflation caused mainly by a rise in total demand that exceeds supply is called:

options.option_text: Cost-push inflation
Demand-pull inflation
Imported inflation
Structural inflation

questions.explanation: Demand-pull — aggregate demand exceeds aggregate supply at current prices. Cost-push — higher input costs (oil, wages) drive prices up. Imported — costlier imports or a weaker currency. Structural — bottlenecks in specific sectors such as food or housing.

questions.stem: The situation of simultaneous high inflation and high unemployment is called:

options.option_text: Recession
Stagflation
Deflation
Reflation

questions.explanation: Stagflation — stagnant output with rising prices — breaks the classic Phillips curve relation. Best-known example: OECD economies in the 1970s after the oil shocks. Reflation = deliberate policy to push prices up after a deflationary spell; deflation = falling prices; recession = two quarters of negative GDP growth.

questions.stem: Which group carries the largest weight in the CPI (Combined) basket in India?

options.option_text: Housing
Food and beverages
Fuel and light
Transport and communication

questions.explanation: Food and beverages accounts for roughly 46 % of the CPI (Combined) basket — which is why food-price shocks dominate headline retail inflation in India. Housing weight applies only to the urban CPI. The rest of the basket is pan/tobacco, clothing, fuel and light, household goods, health, education, transport and miscellaneous.

questions.stem: Hyperinflation, in standard economic literature, is inflation typically exceeding:

options.option_text: 5 % per year
50 % per month
10 % per year
100 % per year

questions.explanation: The classic Cagan threshold for hyperinflation is 50 % per month. Famous cases: Weimar Germany (1923), Hungary (1946, worst ever), Zimbabwe (2008), Venezuela (2016-19). Rough categorisation: creeping < 3 % p.a., walking 3-10 %, galloping 10-100 %, anything faster and accelerating = hyperinflation.

questions.stem: If the RBI wants to reduce inflation through monetary policy, it will typically:

options.option_text: Cut the repo rate
Raise the repo rate
Cut the cash reserve ratio (CRR)
Buy government bonds in the open market

questions.explanation: A higher repo rate raises banks' cost of funds, lifts lending rates, cools borrowing and demand, and eases inflation. Rate cuts, CRR cuts and open-market bond purchases are expansionary and add to inflationary pressure. The repo rate is decided by the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC), a six-member body that meets at least every two months.

questions.stem: Under India's inflation-targeting framework, the RBI has to keep CPI inflation (on average) at:

options.option_text: 2 %, with a ±2 % tolerance band
4 %, with a ±2 % tolerance band
6 %, with a ±2 % tolerance band
5 %, with a ±1 % tolerance band

questions.explanation: Since the 2016 amendment to the RBI Act, India runs a flexible inflation-targeting regime — CPI inflation target is 4 % with a tolerance band of ±2 %, i.e., between 2 % and 6 %. The target is reviewed by the Government in consultation with the RBI every five years; the 4 % target was retained for the 2021-26 period.

questions.stem: A fall in the overall price level over a sustained period is called:

options.option_text: Disinflation
Deflation
Reflation
Stagflation

questions.explanation: Deflation — sustained fall in the general price level. Disinflation is when inflation itself slows (prices still rising, just more slowly). Reflation is the policy effort to push prices back up after a deflationary period. Stagflation is high inflation combined with stagnant growth. Japan's 'lost decades' (1990s-2000s) are the textbook modern deflation example.

questions.stem: What does 'core CPI inflation' in India measure, as distinct from headline CPI inflation?

options.option_text: Price changes in wholesale markets, excluding retail
Price changes excluding food & beverages and fuel & light
Price changes in rural households only, not urban ones
Price changes in manufactured goods and services only

questions.explanation: Core inflation strips out the two most volatile sub-groups — food & beverages and fuel & light — from headline CPI to reveal the underlying, more persistent price trend. Option D is wrong because core inflation also includes services (housing, education, health), not just manufactured goods.

questions.stem: The Wholesale Price Index (WPI) in India is compiled and released by which authority?

options.option_text: Central Statistics Office, Ministry of Statistics
Reserve Bank of India's Department of Statistics
Office of the Economic Adviser, Ministry of Commerce
National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development

questions.explanation: WPI is published by the Office of the Economic Adviser (OEA) under the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT), Ministry of Commerce and Industry. Option A is wrong — CSO/NSO handles CPI and national accounts, not WPI.

questions.stem: Of the six members constituting India's Monetary Policy Committee (MPC), how many are external members nominated by the Union Government?

options.option_text: Two, comprising economists from premier institutions
Four, giving majority control to the government side
One, who acts as the government's sole voting representative
Three, chosen from the fields of economics and finance

questions.explanation: Under Section 45ZB of the RBI Act, the MPC has six members: RBI Governor (Chair), Deputy Governor (monetary policy), one RBI-nominated officer, and three external members appointed by the Central Government. The split is 3 RBI + 3 government, with the Governor casting the deciding vote in a tie. Option B is wrong — the government does not hold majority; it is an equal split.

questions.stem: The term 'skewflation', occasionally used by Indian monetary authorities, describes a situation where:

options.option_text: Both inflation and deflation occur in different regions
Price rise is concentrated in a single sector like food
Wages and prices enter a mutually reinforcing spiral upward
Government suppresses prices through administered price controls

questions.explanation: Skewflation refers to inflation that is skewed toward one sector — most notably food — while other sectors remain relatively stable. Former RBI Governor D. Subbarao used this term around 2009–10 to describe India's food-price surge. Option C describes a wage-price spiral, which is a separate phenomenon.

questions.stem: In the context of inflation measurement, a 'favourable base effect' occurs when:

options.option_text: The current period sees a large surge in supply of essentials
The RBI cuts interest rates to stimulate aggregate demand
Inflation appears lower because the base period had high prices
Government increases the minimum support price for foodgrains

questions.explanation: A favourable base effect occurs when the year-ago (base) period recorded unusually high prices, making the current year-on-year inflation rate appear lower even if prices have not actually fallen. Conversely, an unfavourable base effect occurs when the base period had abnormally low prices, making current inflation appear high. Option A describes a supply-side development, not a statistical base effect.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes the GDP Deflator from the Consumer Price Index (CPI)?

options.option_text: GDP deflator uses a fixed Laspeyres basket; CPI revises its weights automatically
GDP deflator covers only domestically produced goods; CPI also includes imports
GDP deflator weights are fixed at base year; CPI weights shift with output mix
GDP deflator is released every quarter alongside GDP data; CPI is published monthly

questions.explanation: The GDP deflator covers all goods and services produced within the domestic economy (C + I + G + X − M), so imported goods are excluded because they are not part of domestic GDP. CPI, however, includes imported goods that consumers actually purchase. Option A reverses the truth: CPI uses a fixed Laspeyres-type basket, while the GDP deflator (a Paasche index) automatically updates its weights to the current production mix. Option D, though factually accurate about release frequency, is not a conceptual economic distinction.

questions.stem: In 'open inflation', prices rise freely in response to excess demand. Its counterpart — where inflationary pressure exists but prices are prevented from rising — is termed:

options.option_text: Creeping inflation, where prices rise at 1–3% per annum
Repressed or suppressed inflation, held down by price controls
Structural inflation, caused by supply-side bottlenecks in economy
Imported inflation, triggered by rising global commodity prices

questions.explanation: Suppressed (or repressed) inflation occurs when governments use price controls, subsidies, or rationing to prevent open price rises despite underlying inflationary pressure. Once controls are lifted, the pent-up inflation surfaces rapidly. Option C (structural inflation) refers to inflation in developing economies arising from supply rigidities — it is a cause-based classification, not the same as the open/suppressed distinction tested here.
